newsitem.title: USA: Cold winter could put US propane stocks at 15yr low.
newsitem.headline: Cold winter could put US propane stocks at 15yr low.

text.p: A U.S. government official said Wednesday that propane inventories could fall to 15-year lows by the end of the heating season if the country gets a repeat of last year's cold, wet winter.

Speaking at a conference on propane, John Cook of the Energy Information Administration said that propane stocks -- already at lows for this time of year -- could draw down to 17 million barrels by the end of the heating season in March.
"Fifteen million barrels is about as low we can go," added Cook, at the New England Governor's Conference in Manchester.
The propane situation, said Cook, "is more likely to get worse than better."
A severe drop in propane stocks at the end of last winter, combined with strong demand, was largely responsible for the price spikes in what has been a volatile market so far this year.
Propane, a liquefied petroleum gas, is used as a heating fuel for many rural homes in the United States, as well in agriculture and petrochemical production.

"If it's a normal winter, supply should about follow the three-year average and finish the season with 21 milion barrels. But if it's a wet and cold winter inventories can fall to 17 million barrels," said Cook.
According to Dan Lippe, a Houston-based analyst with Petral Consulting Co., a 17 million barrel level in March of 1997 would be the lowest level in 15 years.
"At 17 million barrels, that means there will be some storage facilities that have no propane at all," said Lippe in a phone interview from Texas.

Lippe added that collectively, the industry must keep five to six million barrels stored to prevent their tanks from physically collapsing. These barrels are are still counted by the EIA as propane inventory.
"So some people think the number could be as low as 10 or 11 million barrels," said Lippe.
The market had about 22 million barrels in March last year.

In other comments, Cook said that retail prices of propane are running at about $1.05 a gallon, about 15 percent higher than last October. He said prices could rise another 15 cents if this winter is harsh.
Such a rise would mean about a 15 cents to 25 cents a gallon increase for residential consumers, said Lippe.
-- Michael Ellis, New York Energy Desk 1212-859-1623
